newsitem.title: UK: British don't know their mashed carrot - survey.
newsitem.headline: British don't know their mashed carrot - survey.

text.p: A staggering 70 percent of British consumers blindfolded and asked to identify various foods and drinks could not recognise the flavour of mashed carrot, according to research by chilled juices company Tropicana.
Even with mashed potato, a fifth of those tested could not identify the taste, said the research.
Many people had trouble recognising cooked apples and pears. Forty percent of tasters did not recognise the taste of cooked apples. The figure rose sharply for cooked pears to 68 percent.
More than a third of respondents could not recognise red wine while a quarter had difficulty telling white wine.
"What is certain is that recent discounting of food and drink products has led to the use of poorer quality ingredients and a loss of natural taste," said Tropicana.

The research also showed regional differences in England. Southerners and midlanders had few problems identifying cooked apple, but over half of the respondents in the North-West had no idea about its identity.

"It is clear that the colour and appearance of food is very influential -- the blindfold tests show that consumers have real difficulty in defining taste and become confused in identifying food types when they cannot see what they are eating or drinking," said Lynda Worthy of Tropicana.
